editorial.headline: Non-Rhizome Medicinal Crops, From Fieldwork to Seed
editorial.standfirst: A farming code for non-rhizome medicinal and biofarmaka plants, open across business scales and not blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This activity is the cultivation of non-rhizome medicinal plants: a practical agricultural category for crops such as cardamom, aloe vera, sambiloto, mengkudu or pace, mahkota dewa, and green lemongrass, including comparable plants used for botanical pesticide materials. Its scope is not limited to planting. The record describes a full farming cycle: land preparation, sowing, planting, maintenance, harvesting, and post-harvest work when those steps are carried out as one connected chain. It also reaches seed production by planting non-rhizome medicinal crops to produce seed in the form of grain.

The same scope also captures the cultivation and seed-production work for non-rhizome medicinal or biofarmaka plants named in the record: kina, adas pinang, and gambir. That matters because the code is written around the agricultural operation, not around a single finished product. A founder using it is not merely saying, “we trade herbal ingredients.” The registered activity is the farming process itself: preparing land, raising or propagating plants, maintaining the crop, harvesting it, and handling the immediate post-harvest sequence where it remains part of the same agricultural chain.

On scale, the record is unusually clean: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar are all open. Nationally, the foreign-investment position is also clean. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In plain English, the national record does not impose a foreign-share cap below full ownership for this activity. A foreign-owned company can therefore read the national line as open, provided the real registered business is the cultivation of these non-rhizome medicinal plants and the integrated farming steps described in the scope.

The Bali picture is also honest but not obstructive. The province has a moratorium rule that blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across Bali, island-wide and permanent. This activity, however, is not marked as blocked in the slim record. The reason is specific: at Besar scale, the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not blocked by that moratorium. The result is a straightforward conclusion, without a hidden provincial contradiction: nationally open to PMA up to 100%, open across the listed scales, and in Bali not blocked by the cited moratorium status in this record.
